Grok Bot can now read a sign-in code or link from your connected Gmail or Outlook, or its own inbox, so it doesn't stop to ask you for it.

A Grok Bot can now read a sign-in code from your email on its own. When a website emails you a code or a link to sign in, the Grok Bot reads it from your connected Gmail or Outlook, or from its own inbox, so it does not stop and ask you to type it. The next thing people will notice is how many of their sign-ins now depend on one email account, so that account becomes the one worth protecting first. A Grok Bot with its own @ mail.grokbot .com inbox could turn out to be the cleaner way to handle it.

OpenCode says a large distillation attack drained OpenAI, Anthropic and Google balances for about 1.4% of its console users, who were emailed.

🚨 AI News | TestingCatalog@testingcatalog
OpenCode published an official statement regarding a recent distillation attack.

> Earlier today, OpenAI, Anthropic and Google balances of some OpenCode users got drained.

> Reportedly, only 1.4% of users were affected and these users were notified via an email.

This is a serious precedent because if this distillation vector is the simplest to execute, that means that major AI labs are now much more protected than they were earlier. This also means that using smaller providers is now less safe.

Additionally, tokens from leading AI labs now have a higher value since they are harder to get for distillation.

A wild AI west 👀

04

Checking your agents' work

2 posts
4.4K engagements

Give your agent a way to verify its work. With that in place, Claude Code wrote 90%+ of its own code, and he argues line-by-line human review has to become layered checks like end-to-end tests and agents reviewing each other. Lauren reposted it.

Addy Osmani@addyosmani
Give your agent a way to verify its work. This can dramatically improve the quality of output.

With this process in place, Claude Code was able to write 90%+ of its code itself. When generating software at a faster rate than you can review it, the bottleneck shifts to proving that it works. @bcherny and team invested enough in verification, we've been able to move fast while maintaining stability.

Code reviews aren't going away, but you need to think of it differently. One human reading through line-by-line is no longer going to work as a gate, it needs to evolve into a multi-layered verification system, built with fast deterministic feedback loops for your agents.

This is where e2e tests, feature maps (as @poteto has been advocating), property tests and multi-agent adversarial reviews come in. These all provide opportunities to catch errors early and fix them before things get out of hand.

You don't have enough eyeballs for the amount of code being written so your focus needs to be on product intent, risk assessment and evaluating evidence rather than reviewing code. Delegate the code checking work to your automated tests, scale your approvals based on risk, and turn your test failures into living evaluations. This approach helps maintain speed without losing reliability.

Let the agents do what they do best and let you focus on what makes you irreplaceable: judgement, direction, and ownership. We tried to capture how we handle code review and verification in this writeup. Hopefully it's helpful.
